Parameters

Source: vignettes/v02-parameters.Rmd
v02-parameters.Rmd

Get started introduced params with three examples. This vignette goes deeper: what a param holds, how its rules work, how params are grouped into configs and set in a pipeline, and how they appear in a document. It builds on pipeflow’s vignettes Annotated parameter values (the hook that pubflow’s params use) and Pipeline views.

library(pipeflow)
library(pubflow)

A param is a value with attributes

A param is a value together with attributes that describe it. The functions of a pipeline never see the attributes, they get the plain value.

xVar <- choice_param(
    "Temp.Celsius",
    choices = c("Temp.Celsius", "Wind", "Solar.R"),
    label = "Predictor",
    description = "Variable that explains the ozone concentration",
    source = "user"
)
xVar
# param<factor>: <factor[1]: Temp.Celsius>
#   levels: Temp.Celsius, Wind, Solar.R
#   label: Predictor
#   description: Variable that explains the ozone concentration
#   source: user
#   validity: <function>

The accessors read the value and the attributes:

param_value(xVar)
# [1] Temp.Celsius
# Levels: Temp.Celsius Wind Solar.R
param_type(xVar)
# [1] "factor"
param_attr(xVar, "label")
# [1] "Predictor"

Base functions work on a param as on its value, so xVar == "Wind" and levels(xVar) work as expected. Note that identical(xVar, "Temp.Celsius") is FALSE, because the attributes are part of the object. Hand param_value() to code that expects a plain value.

Besides label and description, pubflow knows the attributes source (e.g. "user" for the params that the user sets), area (a group of params), advanced (shown in a collapsed block), locked (shown as a disabled input, see Locked params) and a few more for the UI. Any other named argument is stored as well. ?param lists all of them.

Constructors and validity

Each constructor comes with a rule that tells whether a value is valid. param_validity() applies it to the param’s own value or to any other value and returns one message per rule, "" meaning valid:

param_validity(xVar)
# [1] ""
param_validity(xVar, value = "Height")
# [1] "value must be one of: Temp.Celsius, Wind, Solar.R"

level <- numeric_param(
    0.95,
    label = "Confidence level",
    min = 0.5,
    max = 0.999,
    source = "user"
)
param_validity(level, value = 1.5)
# [1] "value must be less than or equal to max (0.999)"

numeral_param() is for numbers that must keep their decimal places. A number like 0.90 is 0.9 as soon as it is a number; a numeral holds the text and checks that it can be read as a number, in the given bounds:

limit <- numeral_param("80.0", label = "Ozone limit (ppb)", min = 0)
param_value(limit)
# [1] "80.0"
param_validity(limit, value = "abc")
# [1] "value was not coercible to numeric"
param_validity(limit, value = "-5")
# [1] "value must be greater than or equal to min (0)"

To add a rule of your own, use add_validity(). A rule is a function that takes the plain value and returns "" or a message. It is used in addition to the default rule:

level <- add_validity(level, \(x) {
    if (x != 0.5) "" else "a level of 0.5 is not allowed"
})
param_validity(level, value = 0.5)
# [1] ""                              "a level of 0.5 is not allowed"

A rule that fails with an error counts as a message too, so a faulty rule never breaks a parameter UI. Own constructors for recurring kinds of params, which wrap one of the above, are shown in the examples of ?param.

Groups

param_group() combines params that belong together, here the range of temperatures that the analysis uses. The group is shown side by side in a UI and checked as a whole: each child by its own rule and the group by rules that see all children. Such a rule is added with add_validity() as well:

window <- param_group(
    list(
        from = numeric_param(0, label = "From", min = -20, max = 60),
        to = numeric_param(30, label = "To", min = -20, max = 60)
    ),
    label = "Temperature range (°C)",
    source = "user",
    area = "data"
) |>
    add_validity(\(x) if (x$from < x$to) "" else "'From' must be below 'To'")

param_validity(window)
# group  from    to 
#    ""    ""    ""
param_validity(window, value = list(from = 30, to = 10))
#                       group                        from                          to 
# "'From' must be below 'To'"                          ""                          ""

The result has one element for the group and one per child. A step gets the value of a group as a plain named list, so prep below reads window$from and window$to.

Configs

A config collects the params of an analysis. It numbers the params in the order given (the order of a parameter UI). Combining configs numbers them anew.

base <- param_config(
    xVar = xVar,
    level = level,
    window = window,
    title = param("Ozone in New York", label = "Report title", source = "user")
)
base
# <param_config: 4 params>
#  name   type      value                     label                 
#  xVar   factor    <factor[1]: Temp.Celsius> Predictor             
#  level  numeric   0.95                      Confidence level      
#  window list      <list[2]: from=0, to=30>  Temperature range (°C)
#    from numeric   0                         From                  
#    to   numeric   30                        To                    
#  title  character Ozone in New York         Report title

Configs are combined with c(). Names must be unique, unless you say that the first definition wins. That is useful for a stricter variant of a config, e.g. for a validated analysis, that overrides single params of the base config:

strict <- param_config(
    level = numeric_param(
        0.99,
        label = "Confidence level",
        min = 0.5,
        max = 0.999,
        source = "user",
        locked = TRUE
    )
)
config <- c(strict, base, .duplicates = "first")
names(config)
# [1] "level"  "xVar"   "window" "title"
param_value(config$level)
# [1] 0.99

Params in a pipeline

The analysis is the pipeline of the Get started vignette with a filter on the temperature and a table of the coefficients. The functions are written with plain defaults that equal the values of the config.

The table is made by a function defined outside the pipeline, as in Get started:

coef_table <- function(model, level) {
    ci <- confint(model, level = level)
    coefs <- data.frame(
        term = rownames(ci),
        estimate = coef(model),
        lower = ci[, 1L],
        upper = ci[, 2L]
    )
    pub_table(
        coefs,
        caption = sprintf("Coefficients with %g%% confidence limits", 100 * level),
        labels = c(
            term = "Term",
            estimate = "Estimate",
            lower = "Lower",
            upper = "Upper"
        ),
        digits = c(estimate = 3L, lower = 3L, upper = 3L)
    )
}
pip <- pip_new("ozone") |>
    pip_add("data", function(data = airquality) data) |>
    pip_add(
        "prep",
        function(df = ~data, window = list(from = 0, to = 30)) {
            df[, "Temp.Celsius"] <- (df[, "Temp"] - 32) * 5 / 9
            inRange <- df$Temp.Celsius >= window$from & df$Temp.Celsius <= window$to
            df[inRange, ]
        }
    ) |>
    pip_add("fit", function(data = ~prep, xVar = "Temp.Celsius") {
        lm(paste("Ozone ~", xVar), data = data)
    }) |>
    pip_add("coef_table", function(model = ~fit, level = 0.99) {
        coef_table(model, level)
    })

The last steps add a summary text, a table of the params (explained in A table of parameters) and the layout step:

pip |>
    pip_add("summary", function(model = ~fit, xVar = "Temp.Celsius") {
        pub_text(sprintf(
            "**%s** explains %.0f%% of the variance of the ozone concentration.",
            xVar,
            100 * summary(model)$r.squared
        ))
    }) |>
    pip_add(
        "params_table",
        function(
            xVar = "Temp.Celsius",
            level = 0.99,
            window = list(from = 0, to = 30),
            title = "Ozone in New York"
        ) {
            # the arguments are not used: they make the step run again when
            # one of the reported params changes
            pub_params_table(
                pub_get_params(.self, source = "user"),
                caption = "Parameters of the analysis"
            )
        }
    ) |>
    pip_add(
        "report",
        function(
            title = "Ozone in New York",
            summary = ~summary,
            table = ~coef_table,
            params = ~params_table
        ) {
            pub_doc(
                pub_section("Results", summary, table),
                pub_section("Parameters", params),
                title = title
            )
        }
    )

pip_set_params() sets the params of the config in every step that has an argument of the same name. A step’s plain default has no rules, so this first application stores the params of the config as they are, without a check. Check a config before you apply it: param_validity_assert() signals an error for an invalid entry. After that, every new value is checked against the rules of its param (see below).

invisible(lapply(config, param_validity_assert))

With unknown = "error", a param that no step has is an error instead of a warning:

pip_set_params(pip, config, unknown = "error")
pip
# <pipeflow> ozone (7 steps)
# --------------------------
#            step                     params                         depends state
# 1:         data                       data                                   new
# 2:         prep                  df,window                            data   new
# 3:          fit                  data,xVar                            prep   new
# 4:   coef_table                model,level                             fit   new
# 5:      summary                 model,xVar                             fit   new
# 6: params_table    xVar,level,window,title                                   new
# 7:       report title,summary,table,params summary,coef_table,params_table   new
# --------------------------
# <ready> last run: never
# steps: 7 new
pip_set_params(pip, list(alpha = 0.05), unknown = "error")
# Error:
# ! Trying to set parameters not defined in the target: alpha

The steps still get plain values. pub_get_params() reads the param objects back. It lists them in the order of the config (order = "config", the default) or in the order in which the pipeline first uses the names (order = "pipeline"), and it can filter by attributes:

names(pub_get_params(pip))
# [1] "level"  "xVar"   "window" "title"
names(pub_get_params(pip, order = "pipeline"))
# [1] "window" "xVar"   "level"  "title"
names(pub_get_params(pip, area = "data"))
# [1] "window"

Setting a value that is not valid is an error, and nothing is set. All failures are collected into one error that names step and param:

pip_set_params(
    pip,
    list(xVar = "Height", window = list(from = 30, to = 10))
)
# Error:
# ! Cannot set 5 parameters: nothing was set.
#   step 'prep', parameter 'window': 'From' must be below 'To'
#   step 'fit', parameter 'xVar': value must be one of: Temp.Celsius, Wind, Solar.R
#   step 'summary', parameter 'xVar': value must be one of: Temp.Celsius, Wind, Solar.R
#   step 'params_table', parameter 'xVar': value must be one of: Temp.Celsius, Wind, Solar.R
#   step 'params_table', parameter 'window': 'From' must be below 'To'

Run the pipeline once. A group is set as a list; this changes the data that prep returns, so prep and all steps that depend on it are outdated and run again:

pip_run(pip, lgr = NULL)
pip_set_params(pip, list(window = list(from = 10, to = 25)))
pip
# <pipeflow> ozone (7 steps)
# --------------------------
#            step                     params                         depends    state
# 1:         data                       data                                     done
# 2:         prep                  df,window                            data outdated
# 3:          fit                  data,xVar                            prep outdated
# 4:   coef_table                model,level                             fit outdated
# 5:      summary                 model,xVar                             fit outdated
# 6: params_table    xVar,level,window,title                                 outdated
# 7:       report title,summary,table,params summary,coef_table,params_table outdated
#                                            out
# 1:                         <data.frame[153x6]>
# 2:                         <data.frame[126x7]>
# 3:                                    <lm[13]>
# 4:                             <huxtable[3x4]>
# 5: **Temp.Celsius** explains 28% of the var...
# 6:                             <huxtable[5x3]>
# 7:                                <pub_doc[2]>
# --------------------------
# <ready> last run: 2026-11-12 16:27:10 (0.083 s)
# steps: 1 done, 6 outdated

One value per name

A name has one value in the whole pipeline: xVar is the argument of fit, summary and params_table, and setting it sets all of them. This holds also if the params are set through a view (e.g. the steps that a parameter UI shows). pipeflow’s Pipeline views vignette describes this in detail (pipeflow 0.5.0.9027 or later). With scope = "view" only the steps of the view are set:

xVars <- function(p) {
    sapply(pip_get_params(p, simplify = FALSE)$xVar, as.character)
}

pip_set_params(pip_view(pip, step = "summary"), list(xVar = "Wind"))
xVars(pip)
#          fit      summary params_table 
#       "Wind"       "Wind"       "Wind"

pip_set_params(
    pip_view(pip, step = "summary"),
    list(xVar = "Solar.R"),
    scope = "view"
)
xVars(pip)
#          fit      summary params_table 
#       "Wind"    "Solar.R"       "Wind"

Now summary explains the ozone concentration with another variable than fit, which is rarely intended. pipeflow warns when a step is added or replaced with a param that differs from the same param in the other steps:

copy <- pip_clone(pip)
pip_add(copy, "note", function(level = 0.9) level)
# Warning: Params with the same name have different values, but pip_set_params() sets one value in all steps that have the param:
# - 'level' is 0.9 in step 'note', but 0.99 in step 'coef_table'
# pip_get_params() with simplify = FALSE shows the values of all steps.

Setting the config again puts the params back. (To change the function of a step but keep the current values of its params, use the argument keep_params of pip_replace().)

pip_set_params(pip, config, unknown = "error")
xVars(pip)
#            fit        summary   params_table 
# "Temp.Celsius" "Temp.Celsius" "Temp.Celsius"

A table of parameters

A report documents the params that an analysis used. pub_params_table() makes a table from param objects, by default with their labels, values and descriptions. Other columns are the name or any attribute:

params <- pub_get_params(pip, source = "user")
pub_params_table(params, columns = c(name = "Name", value = "Value", area = "Area")) |>
    pub_cell_text()
#      [,1]     [,2]                [,3]  
# [1,] "Name"   "Value"             "Area"
# [2,] "level"  "0.99"              ""    
# [3,] "xVar"   "Temp.Celsius"      ""    
# [4,] "window" "0, 30"             "data"
# [5,] "title"  "Ozone in New York" ""

The step params_table above puts the table into the document. It reads the param objects of the pipeline through .self, which a step function can use without declaring it. The step lists the params it reports as arguments, so that it runs again when one of them changes. .self bypasses the pipeline’s dependency tracking, so list every param that the table reports: one that is left out can change without the step running again. The layout step takes the table as an input like any other output:

pip_run(pip, lgr = NULL)
pub_html(pip[["report", "out"]])

Locked params

In a validated analysis, some params are fixed, here the confidence level of strict. A param with locked = TRUE is shown in a parameter UI as a disabled input: the user sees the value but can’t change it. The steps run as usual.

param_attr(pub_get_params(pip)$level, "locked")
# [1] TRUE

The lock binds the UI only. Code can still change a locked param, subject to its validity rules:

pip_set_params(pip, list(level = 0.9))
param_value(pub_get_params(pip)$level)
# [1] 0.9

pipeflow’s step locks (pip_lock()) are different: a locked step no longer runs, pip_set_params() skips it, and the UI shows its params as locked too. To fix params but keep the steps running, use the attribute.
